articles.summary:
Israeli rabbi says politicians cooperating with Arab parties can be killed

A prominent rabbi in Israel has invoked a Jewish religious doctrine permitting the use of lethal force against politicians who cooperate with Arab parties, Haaretz reported.

Rabbi Gedalya Axelrod, a former head of the Haifa Rabbinical Court, said in a handwritten ruling that Jewish party leaders who support a government formed with the backing of Arab parties are subject to din rodef, or the “law of the pursuer”. 

Axelrod wrote that collaboration with Arab parties "poses a terrible danger to the people of Israel in the Holy Land and around the world".

Under Jewish religious law, a rodef is someone who poses a threat to another person's life and may be stopped by any means necessary. The doctrine was invoked by Yitzhak Rabin’s assassin, Yigal Amir, to justify the prime minister’s killing in 1995.

articles.title: Israel extends $3,500 departure grant to nationals of all African countries
articles.summary:
Israel extends $3,500 departure grant to nationals of all African countries

Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 11/13/2026 - 11:39
Officials hope payment will bring number of departure back up after resettlement routes to Canada and the United States narrowed
In this file photo, residents of the southern district of the Israeli city of Tel Aviv protest against the presence of African refugees and asylum seekers on 30 August 2018 (AFP)
Off

Israel is extending its $3,500 voluntary departure grant to nationals of every African country in a bid to reverse a decline in the number of migrants leaving with state assistance, according to Haaretz.

Until now the payment had been limited mainly to people from a handful of states. 

The change took effect on Monday and will remain in place until the end of the year, Israel's Population and Immigration Authority said. Applications must be submitted by 31 December.

It covers African nationals who have stayed in Israel for more than two years without a valid visa, and those holding temporary residency permits. 

For the first time, it also includes people who entered Israel legally but overstayed their visas.

The authority expects several thousand more people to be eligible, including citizens of Nigeria, South Africa and Togo.

Before the change, the grant was mostly open to people who crossed into Israel outside official border points. That group includes nationals of Eritrea, Sudan, Ethiopia, Ivory Coast and Guinea, along with citizens of countries that have no diplomatic relations with Israel.

The authority’s figures show that 3,511 African nationals left with help from its Voluntary Departure Unit in 2024. That fell to 2,815 in 2025, a drop of about 20 percent. 

In its 2025 annual report, the authority blamed smaller asylum quotas in Canada, the closure of US borders to asylum seekers, and war-related airspace closures that disrupted flights.

Eritreans made up 89 percent of African departures through the scheme last year. According to the authority’s data, about 90 percent of Eritreans and Sudanese who left went to countries outside Africa. Around two percent returned to their home countries.

Shrinking options

The grant is the same amount Israel offered in 2018.

That year, under then-prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the government gave about 38,000 mostly Eritrean and Sudanese asylum seekers a choice: leave for an unnamed third country with $3,500 and a plane ticket, or face imprisonment.

Israel arrests and plans to deport Ethiopian asylum seekers
Read More »

The plan was abandoned in April 2018 after Netanyahu scrapped a UN resettlement deal.

Israel’s refugee recognition rate is under 0.1 percent, according to a December 2025 report by the Forum of Refugee and Asylum Seeker Organizations in Israel.

The forum estimates that about 13,000 Eritreans and 6,700 Sudanese are in Israel under group protection from deportation.

In August, the interior ministry said it would grant temporary residency to Sudanese asylum seekers who had applied by June 2025.

Refugee aid group HIAS called the decision “a direct result of relentless legal pressure”.

Ethiopians have lost protection altogether. After Israel’s high court upheld the government’s withdrawal of their group protection in December 2025, authorities began arresting Ethiopian asylum seekers in March and planned to start deportations in April, MEE reported.

The aid group Assaf estimated that about 8,000 Ethiopians faced deportation, around 1,000 of them from Tigray.

In June, police arrested Eritreans in Tel Aviv under a 2025 law allowing deportation of people identified as supporters of the Eritrean government.

articles.title: Denmark pledges $8.9m in aid for Gaza amid severe winter flooding
articles.summary:
Denmark pledges $8.9m in aid for Gaza amid severe winter flooding

Denmark has announced $8.9m in humanitarian aid for Palestinians, including an emergency allocation to help people affected by flooding in Gaza.

The Danish Foreign Ministry said it would provide 20 million kroner ($3m) to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa, to help those affected by severe winter weather. 

“Severe winter weather is worsening the crisis in Palestine,” Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said. 

“We must ensure that essential humanitarian aid reaches the affected population during the winter months.”

Denmark also pledged a further 40 million kroner ($6m) to the Occupied Palestinian Territory Humanitarian Fund, which mainly supports humanitarian operations in Gaza, where heavy rains have flooded displacement camps.

articles.title: Israeli police deploy rooftop snipers in Bedouin city of Rahat
articles.summary:
Israeli police deploy rooftop snipers in Bedouin city of Rahat

Israeli police have stationed snipers on rooftops in Rahat, a Bedouin city in southern Israel, saying they would “neutralise” gunmen who open fire.

The deployment follows reports of heavy daytime gunfire and the reported discovery of weapons caches in the area. 

Rahat Mayor Talal al-Kernawi said the city had experienced clashes involving six families over the past month, in which two young people were killed.

“In recent days there has been nonstop gunfire that is endangering the lives of innocent civilians who are not involved in the conflicts,” he told Haaretz.
